title: Does the Flipped Classroom Lead to Increased Gains of Learning Outcomes in ESL/EFL Contexts?
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a flipped classroom model improves student learning outcomes in ESL/EFL grammar instruction compared with a nonflipped, in-class lecture format. It also examines whether students’ attitudes toward their grammar abilities change over time and whether students show buy-in to the flipped approach.

The intervention was a flipped grammar curriculum built around teacher-recorded video lessons, short online quizzes, and discussion-post activities completed outside class. In the control condition, students received the same grammar content through in-class mini-lectures and practice quizzes. The study used a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental mixed-methods design with 64 learners across two higher-education contexts: a university in Macau, China, and a two-year community college in the United States. The Macau group consisted of first-year undergraduates in intermediate EAP, and the US group consisted of high-intermediate ESL students in developmental/academic writing courses.

Quantitative data came from a 32-item grammar test and a 4-item grammar confidence survey; qualitative data came from student focus groups and assignment-completion patterns. The results showed significant gains on grammar achievement for the flipped classes, while both flipped and nonflipped groups reported improved confidence over time. Focus-group themes suggested that the flipped model increased grammatical awareness, autonomy, and perceived improvement. The authors conclude that flipping can be a viable approach for ESL/EFL grammar instruction, but they recommend gradual implementation and careful design to avoid overburdening students.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental mixed-methods study, but it is not randomized and has a small sample (N=64) across two contexts. The design supports moderate confidence in descriptive and associational claims, but not high causal certainty.
impact_tier_rationale: The flipped grammar intervention showed a modest-to-medium positive effect on achievement (partial η2=.11) in a priority ESL/EFL population. The practical impact is promising but limited by the small sample and context-specific implementation conditions.

interventions.use_case: flipped grammar instruction in ESL/EFL classes using teacher-recorded video lessons, online quizzes, and discussion posts to replace in-class mini-lectures

finding.finding_summary: The flipped condition produced significantly higher gains on grammar achievement than the nonflipped condition in a quasi-experimental study of N=64 ESL/EFL learners. On the 32-item grammar test, the experimental group increased from M=65.85 to M=71.77, while the control group remained essentially flat (M=62.68 to 62.75); the ANOVA showed a significant flipped/nonflipped effect, F(1,62)=7.66, p=.007, partial η2=.11, and a significant interaction with time, F(1,62)=6.69, p=.012, partial η2=.10.
finding.std_deviation: Control pretest SD=9.93, posttest SD=9.74; Experimental pretest SD=10.51, posttest SD=8.45

finding.finding_summary: Both flipped and nonflipped groups reported statistically significant improvements in perceived grammar confidence/comfort over time on a 3-item Likert grammar survey, indicating increased self-efficacy regardless of condition. The control group changed from M=3.14 to 2.74 (Z=2.60, p=.009) and the experimental group from M=2.85 to 2.54 (Z=2.92, p=.004); however, the control group showed the larger correlation change (R=.589 vs .424), so the flipped condition did not outperform the comparison group on this self-report outcome.
finding.measure: 4-item grammar confidence survey, analyzed as 3 items after dropping one problematic item; pre/post self-reported comfort/confidence with grammar

finding.finding_summary: Focus groups with the flipped classes indicated improved learner autonomy, grammatical consciousness-raising, and perceived self-directed improvement from video-based grammar study. In addition, implementation data showed substantial buy-in/compliance with the flipped tasks: 77.75% of all flipped grammar assessments were completed on average, with higher completion in Macau (83%) than the US (72.5%).
finding.measure: Focus-group themes; completion rates for online quizzes and discussion posts
finding.study_size: n=9 focus-group participants; completion data from flipped classes within n=39 experimental students
